newsitem.title: USA: Ford October sales rise on strength of light trucks.
newsitem.headline: Ford October sales rise on strength of light trucks.

text.p: Ford Motor Co. reported a 2.7 percent increase in U.S. sales for October on Wednesday as an expanded line-up of pickup trucks and sport utility vehicles enabled the automaker to overcome slumping car demand.
Ford, the last of the Big Three U.S. automakers to report October results, posted an 8.3 percent increase in sales of domestically produced light trucks to 191,399 units.

Contributing to the surge were combined sales of the Ford Explorer and two new sport utility models, the Expedition and Mercury Mountaineer, of 55,924. That marked a 34 percent jump from a year ago and was a Ford record for monthly sport utility sales, the company said.

Sales of North American-built cars fell 2.9 percent to 140,806. Ford's total unit sales for the month were 334,590. All percentages are based on a daily selling rate. October had 27 selling days, compared with 26 in October 1995.

"As the sport utility market continues to grow dramatically, we're very pleased with the incrementality that our expanded (sport utility) line-up clearly is producing for our dealers and the company," Robert Rewey, Ford group vice president of marketing and sales, said in a statement.

Ford's results lifted total industry sales to 1,270,216, a 2.2 percent increase on a daily-sales-rate basis from 1,196,262 last year. The seasonally adjusted annual sales rate for the month was 14.9 million units, slightly lower than some analysts had predicted.

Analysts warned, however, the actual sales rate was about 14.6 million units because factors provided by the Commerce Department to compute the rate inflates the October number by about 300,000 units.
The slowing sales pace -- the September rate was 15.02 million and August 15.8 million -- had been expected by analysts following strong demand in the first half of the year.

Results at the U.S. No. 2 automaker came in the middle for the Big Three in October. Last week, General Motors Corp. reported that weak car sales dragged down October results by 7.7 percent to 399,382 units. Chrysler Corp., breaking a record for October sales, reported an 18.6 percent increase to 205,393.
Ford's overall numbers were again bolstered by its popular F-Series pickup trucks. Ford sold 72,061 of the pickups in the month, an 8.5 percent increase that was the best October since 1977.
"Overall for Ford, we've seen the F-Series and Explorer has really been carrying them for some time," said Lincoln Merrihew, an analyst at DRI-McGraw Hill Inc.

Although Ford's Explorer sales fell 1.4 percent on a daily selling rate from a year ago, the 38,134 vehicles sold set a record for October. Helping the sales were first-ever marketing incentives that Ford put on the Explorer in September.

But the marketing expenses on the Explorer should be more than offset by hefty profits on the new Expedition full-size sport utility. Ford sold 13,984 of the Expeditions and a small number of carry-over 1996 model Broncos in October.
"I'm sure for every $500 they put on the Explorer they more than make up for it on the Expedition," Merrihew said.
Ford's incentive and marketing efforts to push its Taurus sedan to the top of the U.S. car market are paying off. In October, Ford sold 36,644 Tauruses, a 26.6 percent increase.
The rival for the top-selling car in America, Honda Motor Co. Ltd.'s Accord, sold 36,062 vehicles in October. Taurus also leads Accord in year-to-date sales, 332,060 vs. 320,609.

Jaguar, Ford's luxury car division, said it sold 2,254 units, a jump of 63.2 percent. Jaguar said 50 special editions of the new XK8 offered through the Neiman Marcus catalog sold out within 72 hours of the catalogs arriving in the mail.
Other automakers reporting Tuesday were Volkswagen of America Inc., where sales rose 35.1 percent to 10,030, and Audi of America Inc., which had an 11.5 percent rise to 2,170.
